q: The Sesia river divides Alto Piemonte's two DOCGs between separate provinces. Which of them lies on the western bank?
exp: Gattinara sits west of the Sesia in the province of Vercelli, Ghemme east of it in Novara. Both are Nebbiolo, called Spanna here, and both may be softened with a little Vespolina or Uva Rara.

q: Pink acidic volcanic rock left by a collapsed supervolcano underlies the vineyards at Boca. What is that rock called?
exp: The Valsesia caldera collapsed and tipped on its side, which exposed the whole plumbing of a volcano at the surface. Porphyry soils are acidic and iron-rich, and the Nebbiolo grown on them comes out paler and more savoury than in the Langhe.

q: Ungrafted vines on low pergolas above a thousand metres beneath Mont Blanc are planted to which white grape?
exp: Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle is among the highest vineyard land in Europe, and the altitude is what has kept phylloxera out. The pergolas are kept knee-high so the stone underneath radiates warmth back at the fruit.

q: Stone-pillared pergolas terrace a steep Nebbiolo vineyard at Piedmont's northern boundary with Valle d'Aosta. Which denomination is made there?
exp: The masonry pillars, called pilun, store the day's heat and give it back at night in a place that is marginal for the grape. Everything is worked by hand on terraces too narrow for a machine.

q: Crossing out of Piedmont into Valle d'Aosta, Nebbiolo changes name once again. What is it called there?
exp: Donnas is the valley's Nebbiolo denomination, sitting just upstream of Carema on the same stretch of the Dora Baltea. Chiavennasca in Valtellina and Spanna in Alto Piemonte are the other regional names for the identical grape.

q: A white variety shared with the Swiss Valais gives Valle d'Aosta a saline, high-acid wine of real concentration. Name that grape.
exp: The upper Rhone and the upper Dora Baltea sit either side of the same Alpine watershed, and varieties crossed the passes long before borders mattered. Cornalin made the same journey and is the Valais's Humagne Rouge, while Fumin and Petit Rouge are Aosta natives.

q: One Franciacorta style is bottled at lower pressure and may use no black grapes at all. What is it called?
exp: Saten is made only from Chardonnay and Pinot Bianco and finished under about five atmospheres rather than six, which softens the mousse. It is always Brut, so the silkiness comes from pressure and blend rather than from sugar.

q: Sassella, Grumello, Inferno and Valgella are named subzones of one Lombard denomination. Which one?
exp: Maroggia is the fifth. All five sit on the south-facing terraces of the Adda valley, where Nebbiolo is called Chiavennasca and every operation is done by hand.

q: In the Oltrepo Pavese a red sold as Bonarda is pressed from a differently named variety. Which grape is actually in the bottle?
exp: The true Bonarda Piemontese is a separate grape grown further west, and the two are regularly confused on a list. Oltrepo Bonarda is Croatina, usually frizzante, soft and faintly bitter.

q: Franciacorta's Riserva tier demands a very long stay on the lees before disgorgement. How long?
exp: Riserva must also be vintage-dated, so the ageing and the harvest statement travel together. A non-vintage Franciacorta needs eighteen months on lees and a Millesimato thirty.

q: The white grown on clay flats at the southern end of Lake Garda goes under a local name, though DNA work has tied it to Verdicchio. Name it.
exp: Lugana was long labelled Trebbiano di Lugana, which invited the assumption that it belonged with the undistinguished Trebbiano Toscano. It does not: the grape is Verdicchio, and the heavy clay is what gives the wine its weight and its capacity to age.

q: Dried Moscato grapes make a sweet red with a DOCG of its own in a single commune near Bergamo. Name the wine.
exp: The variety is a dark-berried Moscato found essentially nowhere else, dried on racks and then aged for two years. The zone is measured in tens of hectares, so bottles rarely leave the province.

q: Nebbiolo dried in ventilated lofts through the autumn gives Valtellina a red of at least fourteen percent alcohol. Name that wine.
exp: Sfursat is the dialect form and appears on plenty of labels. Both it and Amarone are legally dry, each disciplinare capping residual sugar, and the fourteen percent floor here is written into the rules.

q: Franciacorta sits on stony debris pushed into low hills by a glacier retreating from Lake Iseo. What is that landform called?
exp: The amphitheatre of moraine drains hard and warms early, which suits early-picked base wine for sparkling. Lugana on the other side of the lake district sits on the heavy clay the same glaciers left behind instead.

q: A large-berried Valpolicella grape was long taken for a clone of Corvina and proved to be a variety in its own right. Which is it?
exp: Corvinone ripens later and holds thicker skins, which is why growers value it for drying. The rules now let it stand in for a share of the Corvina in the blend.

q: Besides Classico, only one valley name may be added to a Valpolicella label. Which name?
exp: Valpantena runs north from Verona just east of the Classico hills and has its own long-standing reputation. Negrar and Marano are Classico communes and Illasi lies in the eastern valleys, but none of them may appear as a denomination on its own.
